cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: Bessel function J at x=1.9, order 2
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.329925829, but that figure is WRONG in the 7th decimal place. Re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: besselj(2, 1.9) = 0.32992572769238721660 (scipy.special.jv agrees to machine precision), which differs from the published 0.329925829 by 1.01e-07 -- far larger than the ~1e-10 rounding residue seen on the sibling BESSELY page. Asserting at 6 dp (0.329926) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the mathematically correct value still agree, so this case tests the function rather than Microsoft's typo

cases.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
cases.expected_note: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 2.7 must behave exactly as order 2. Independently verified with mpmath: besselj(2, 1.9) = 0.3299257276923872, while a genuine fractional-order besselj(2.7, 1.9) would be about 0.16248, so this case separates truncation from fractional-order evaluation

cases.description: The order-0 Bessel function at the origin
cases.expected_note: Follows from the documented series definition on the page: J_0(0) is the k=0 term (-1)^0/(0! * Gamma(1)) * (0/2)^0 = 1, with every later term carrying a positive power of x/2 and vanishing. Independently verified with mpmath: besselj(0, 0) = 1.0 exactly
Excel documents: "If n < 0, BESSELJ returns the #NUM! error value."
Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELJ returns the #VALUE! error value."
